Title: Association of high-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation with 6-month cognitive outcomes and white matter lesion progression in patients with cerebral small vessel disease and cognitive impairment
Aim: Assess whether 10 Hz rTMS over the left DLPFC relates to six-month cognitive outcomes and white matter lesion progression in small vessel disease.
Primary methods: Retrospective cohort of 427 patients (228 rTMS, 199 medication-only) with complete data; primary outcome was change in MoCA; propensity-matched sensitivity analysis.
Results: The rTMS group gained more on MoCA (mean difference 1.11), with better MMSE, TMT-B and delayed recall; no imaging difference was significant.
Discussion: Cognitive benefit may come from plasticity and network changes rather than from slowing lesion growth.
Caveats: Retrospective and based on routine care; subgroup findings are exploratory.

Title: Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation (tDCS) and Smoking Cessation: Clinical and Neurocognitive Outcomes Among Turkish Adults
Aim: Test whether anodal tDCS over the left DLPFC helps smokers quit, and whether it changes executive function.
Primary methods: Active versus sham tDCS in smokers with high nicotine dependence, one session per day, five days a week for two weeks; executive tests before and after; weekly follow-up for a month.
Results: No significant group difference in smoking outcomes or clinical measures after adjusting for baseline imbalance, and no difference on executive tests.
Discussion: tDCS was not effective for smoking cessation here, and the null executive result runs against the wider DLPFC literature.
Caveats: Modest sample; baseline groups differed on smoking measures; context may differ from other populations.

Title: Changes in the Cutaneous Silent Period Following Pallidal Deep Brain Stimulation in Patients with Cervical Dystonia
Aim: Track spinal inhibition, measured by the cutaneous silent period, before and after pallidal DBS in cervical dystonia.
Primary methods: 18 patients measured before and after bilateral GPi-DBS, compared with 18 matched healthy controls.
Results: Silent-period end latency and duration increased early after surgery while stimulation was on; neither timepoint differed from controls, and changes did not track clinical improvement.
Discussion: Spinal inhibition appears to shift dynamically during active DBS, linked to wider motor-network modulation.
Caveats: Small sample; short-term follow-up; no correlation with clinical gains.

Title: Effects of STN-DBS on voluntary facial mimicry in Parkinson's patients: a pilot study
Aim: Test whether subthalamic DBS changes voluntary facial expressiveness in Parkinson's disease.
Primary methods: 18 patients recorded in stimulation-on and stimulation-off states (both on medication) while posing six basic emotions and neutral; facial action units were scored automatically.
Results: Motor scores improved with stimulation. Mimicry was weaker with stimulation off for neutral, happiness, fear and anger, and stronger for sadness.
Discussion: Subthalamic DBS seems to shape emotional motor output beyond classic motor control, which may help social communication.
Caveats: Pilot size; a single within-patient comparison.

Title: Applications of non-invasive brain stimulation in the treatment of children with cerebral palsy: a narrative review
Aim: Summarise evidence for tDCS and rTMS in children with cerebral palsy.
Primary methods: Narrative review informed by a structured literature search.
Results: Small to moderate trials suggest added benefit for gross motor function, gait, balance, spasticity and some cognitive and communication outcomes when paired with rehabilitation; short-term safety was acceptable.
Discussion: Targets include primary motor, dorsolateral prefrontal and language cortex, with plasticity-based mechanisms and individualised protocols.
Caveats: Not systematic; safety data are short-term.

Title: Right putaminal gray matter change tracks psychomotor recovery after accelerated iTBS in melancholic treatment-resistant depression
Aim: Test whether putamen volume change tracks early psychomotor recovery after accelerated theta-burst stimulation (iTBS) in melancholic treatment-resistant depression.
Primary methods: Structural MRI (voxel-based morphometry) in 61 patients and 77 controls, then a double-blind, sham-controlled trial of 20 sessions over four days; 50 patients had complete data.
Results: Patients had more right putamen volume at baseline. After active stimulation, putamen increase tracked psychomotor improvement, but not overall depression, and the link was absent after sham.
Discussion: The authors frame the change as a possible marker of early psychomotor recovery, not as structural normalisation.
Caveats: Correlational; 25 patients per arm; the psychomotor link is a secondary pattern.

Title: The Pallidothalamic Tract in Functional Neurosurgery: A Systematic Review
Aim: Synthesise outcomes of interventions targeting the pallidothalamic tract.
Primary methods: PRISMA 2020, PROSPERO-registered; 40 studies and 483 patients across five modalities, including MR-guided focused ultrasound, DBS, radiofrequency and lesioning.
Results: Average UPDRS-III improvement of 39% in Parkinson's disease, 57% on BFMDRS in dystonia, and seizure reduction in 71% of drug-resistant epilepsy patients.
Discussion: Dual-target strategies may add benefit, and prospective trials are needed to confirm efficacy and safety.
Caveats: Mostly small uncontrolled studies; inconsistent adverse-event reporting.

Title: Dopamine amplifies subthalamic long-latency responses to cortical stimulation in patients with Parkinson's disease
Aim: Determine how dopamine affects signal flow along the cortico-subthalamic hyperdirect pathway.
Primary methods: Bidirectional stimulation with invasive recordings in 15 patients undergoing DBS surgery, across medication states.
Results: The short-latency hyperdirect response was unchanged by medication; later responses were amplified by dopamine; subthalamic-to-cortex responses were unchanged.
Discussion: Fast and slow components of cortex-basal ganglia communication are affected differently by dopamine.

Title: Deep-brain Neuromodulation in Parkinson's Disease: Convergent Mechanisms and Translational Stratification of Deep Brain Stimulation and Low-intensity Focused Ultrasound
Aim: Compare DBS and low-intensity focused ultrasound as deep-brain approaches in Parkinson's disease, looking at mechanisms.
Primary methods: Mechanistic and translational review of clinical and preclinical evidence.
Results: The two share some mechanisms, including network modulation, synaptic remodelling and reduced neuroinflammation. DBS has far stronger clinical evidence.
Discussion: Deep-brain neuromodulation should be viewed as one multi-dimensional framework, with biomarkers and standard endpoints needed.
Caveats: A narrative review, not systematic; clinical ultrasound evidence is still limited.

Title: Implantation of autologous peripheral nerve tissue to the nucleus basalis of Meynert in patients with Parkinson's disease during deep brain stimulation surgery: a 2-year report
Aim: Assess the safety, feasibility and clinical response of placing a nerve graft in the nucleus basalis during DBS surgery.
Primary methods: Seven patients had pallidal DBS plus a sural nerve graft to the nucleus basalis, followed at six-month intervals for up to two years (five completed 24 months).
Results: No serious related adverse events; cognition matched standard DBS patients; motor and quality-of-life scores were slightly worse, with small non-motor gains.
Discussion: The procedure appears safe and feasible without a substantial added cognitive risk, and the authors suggest possible target-specific effects.
Caveats: Seven patients, no control group, and fewer patients at 24 months.

Title: Outcomes of Bilateral Globus Pallidus Internus Deep Brain Stimulation in GNAO1-Related Disorder: An International Multicenter Experience
Aim: Define the impact of bilateral pallidal DBS in GNAO1-related movement disorder, the largest cohort to date.
Primary methods: Retrospective multicentre cohort of 46 patients across 17 centres, with a mean follow-up of 4.5 years; primary outcome was dyskinetic crisis burden.
Results: Crises fell in 38 of 40 patients, and motor scores improved by about 27.5%; complications occurred in 19.6%, mostly in emergency implants.
Discussion: DBS works mainly to prevent crises and reduce overall burden, rather than restoring function, which supports earlier elective surgery.
Caveats: Retrospective; functional classification was largely unchanged.

Title: Deep brain stimulation of the nucleus accumbens for severe self-injurious behaviour in children: long-term outcomes from a first-in-human pilot trial
Aim: Report long-term outcomes of accumbens DBS for severe self-injury in children with autism.
Primary methods: Single-centre first-in-human trial: six participants aged 7–14, bilateral implantation, followed for at least 24 months (mean 32.5).
Results: Self-injury frequency and severity fell and stayed low; one device infection led to relapse, which reversed after re-implantation.
Discussion: Modulating reward circuitry may durably change maladaptive behaviour in childhood neurodevelopmental disorders.
Caveats: Six patients; single centre; the withdrawal-rechallenge evidence rests on one participant.

Title: Deep brain stimulation of the nucleus basalis magnocellularis ameliorates autistic behavior in a rat model of autism via cholinergic modulation in the prefrontal cortex
Aim: Test whether stimulating the nucleus basalis magnocellularis improves autism-like behaviour in a prenatal valproic-acid rat model.
Primary methods: Male offspring were split into control, VPA, implanted-only and stimulated groups; stimulation ran two hours a day for two weeks, with behaviour tests and acetylcholinesterase and choline acetyltransferase staining.
Results: Stimulation improved social behaviour and increased acetylcholinesterase-positive neurons in the medial prefrontal cortex.
Discussion: The benefit is linked to cholinergic signalling in prefrontal cortex, supporting a basal-forebrain route for DBS effects.
Caveats: Animal model; small groups (five saline controls, 16 VPA-exposed rats); the marker link is correlational.

Title: Treatment-characteristic brain structural changes in depression: a multi-center longitudinal observational study
Aim: Compare how grey matter volume changes across four depression treatments: medication, CBT, ECT and rTMS.
Primary methods: 155 patients and 152 controls with MRI at three timepoints; voxel-based morphometry with ComBat scanner harmonisation.
Results: Only ECT and medication changed grey matter over time; CBT and rTMS did not, although all four groups improved clinically. Later left insula loss correlated with worsening on medication.
Discussion: Treatments leave different structural signatures, and the insula could serve as a long-term biomarker.
Caveats: Observational design; the rTMS arm had only 20 patients.
